To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adsorption to soils is well correlated to KOW and that the adsorption to lake sediments is well correlated to solubility.

the adsorption coefficient (KOC) can be estimated from either the KOW or the solubility, but the correlation is not as good as the correlation of KOW with solubility, and that KOC for soils and lake sedents are similar.

the adsorption of chemicals to soils is related to their octanol/water distribution coefficient and their solubility, and that the relationship between adsorption and solubility is different for soils and lake sedents.

understanding the factors controlling the distribution of organic compounds in the environment, and the development of methods to assess the environmental fate of chemicals.
the sorption of organic compounds in the soil environment.
the fate of chemicals in the environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the sorption behaviour of chemicals is dependent on the chemical and physical properties of the chemical and the soil or sediment.
adsorption of chemicals by sediments and soils is a complex phenomenon and that no simple generalization is possible.
the adsorption of organic chemicals by sediments can be predicted from their chemical structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the sorption of non-ionic organic substances to soil and sediment is a function of the solubility of the substance and its affinity for the organic fraction of soil and sediment.
adsorption on soils can be estimated from solubility and KOW data.
the adsorption of chemicals to soils is predictable from their KOW, and that the KOW can be estimated from their solubility.
The main takeaway from our work is that
adsorption of chemicals on organic matter in sediments and soils can be predicted with reasonable accuracy using the solubility and octanol/water distribution coefficients of these chemicals.
adsorption of organic compounds by soils and sedements can be estimated with some confidence from solubility or partition coefficient data.
it is important to use soils and sediments that have been exposed to the same contaminants in order to make meaningful comparisons between the two.
